mainTopic: Meat absorbing dairy or blood: produce cut with a meat knife, salt and vinegar near dairy, a bird fallen into כמכא, bread soaked with meat juice, and catching drippings from roasting meat.
overview: This amud finishes a discussion about vegetables cut with a meat knife and then eaten with כותח, a salty dairy dip. A sharp radish soaks up the meat, but a cucumber only needs the cut spot scraped. Turnip stalks are fine and chard is not. Next, רב נחמן rules that a jar of salt may not stand next to a jar of dairy כמכא, but a jar of vinegar may, because dairy stays in salt and dissolves in vinegar. Then a young bird falls into כמכא and is permitted, because the dip is salty but still edible, so שמואל's rule that salted food is like boiling food does not apply. That leniency covers only a raw bird. A roasted bird needs peeling, and a cracked or spiced bird is fully forbidden. שמואל rules that bread that meat was cut on is forbidden, but only under three conditions, and the גמרא tells how שמואל, רב הונא and רבא handled such bread. Last, שמואל forbids putting a dish under roasting meat until its redness is gone. רב אשי rejects the smoke sign and begins a remedy using two lumps of salt, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Sharp radish absorbs, but a cucumber only needs scraping
steps.stepSummary: A radish cut with a meat knife soaks in the meat because of its sharpness. A cucumber only needs the cut spot scraped before it is eaten with כותח.
steps.simpleTranslation: For because of its sharpness it soaks up the meat. But a cucumber: you scrape the place where it was cut and eat it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a rule from the previous page. A radish cut with a meat knife cannot be eaten with כותח, but a cucumber can if you scrape the cut.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The difference depends on how sharp the vegetable is. A sharp radish pulls the meat taste from the knife deep inside, so scraping won't help. A mild cucumber only has meat on its surface, so scraping removes it.

keyTerms.meaning: Sharpness, a sharp or biting taste
The place where it was cut

steps.confusionAlert: The first words, 'because of its sharpness it absorbs,' are the end of a sentence that started on the previous page. 'It' means the radish.

phrases.english: for because of its sharpness it absorbs,
phrases.notes: 'It' is the radish from the end of the previous page, cut with a meat knife. It soaks up the meat from the blade.

phrases.english: but a cucumber –
one scrapes the place of its cut and eats it.
phrases.notes: He means you may then eat the cucumber with the dairy כותח.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאַגַּב חוּרְפֵּיהּ בָּלַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a ruling begun on the previous page about a radish cut with a meat knife.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A sharp radish cut with a meat knife absorbs meat and may not be eaten with כותח. A cucumber may be eaten with it once the cut area is scraped.

steps.title: Turnip stalks are permitted, chard is forbidden, and alternating makes it fine
steps.stepSummary: Turnip stalks cut with a meat knife may be eaten with כותח, and chard may not. If you cut chard and turnip back and forth, it is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: Turnip stalks are permitted. Chard is forbidden. And if he alternated, cutting turnip in between, it is fine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives more examples of vegetables cut with a meat knife: which may be eaten with כותח and which may not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Chard soaks up taste from the knife, but turnip stalks do not. When turnip is cut in between, the turnip takes away the meat taste on the blade, so the chard cut after it is fine.

phrases.english: turnip stalks – are permitted,
those of chard – are forbidden,
and if he alternated turnip among them –
phrases.notes: He switched back and forth, cutting turnip between the pieces of chard.

phrases.english: it is fine.

steps.triggerLanguage: קִילְחֵי דְּלִיפְתָּא שְׁרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds more vegetable cases to the knife rule from step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Turnip stalks cut with a meat knife are permitted with כותח and chard is forbidden. Cutting turnip in between the chard makes the chard permitted.

steps.title: May a jar of salt stand next to a jar of dairy כמכא?
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי asks רב נחמן whether a jar of salt may be placed next to a jar of כמכא. רב נחמן says it is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב דימי asked רב נחמן: May one place a jar of salt next to a jar of כמכא? He said to him: It is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic starts. רב דימי asks whether a jar of salt may sit next to a jar of dairy dip, and רב נחמן forbids it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry is that a little כמכא might splash into the salt without anyone noticing. Later that salt might be used on meat and mix dairy into it.

keyTerms.meaning: A dairy dip, the same as כותח

phrases.aramaic: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב דִּימִי מֵרַב נַחְמָן:
phrases.english: Rav Dimi asked Rav Naḥman:
what is the law about placing a jar of salt
next to a jar of kamka?
phrases.notes: כמכא is a dairy dip, like כותח. The salt is the kind used for salting meat.

phrases.english: He said to him: It is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּעָא מִינֵּיהּ רַב דִּימִי מֵרַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new question about storing meat seasonings near dairy.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a jar of salt may stand next to a jar of dairy כמכא.

steps.title: What about a jar of vinegar?
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי asks about vinegar placed next to כמכא. רב נחמן says it is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: What about vinegar? He said to him: It is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: רב דימי asks the same question about a jar of vinegar, and this time רב נחמן allows it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case looks the same as salt, since dairy could fall into the vinegar too. Yet the answer is the opposite, which sets up the next question about why.

phrases.english: What about one of vinegar?
phrases.notes: He means a jar of vinegar standing next to the כמכא.

phrases.english: He said to him: It is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּחַלָּא מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A follow-up question with a contrasting case.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a jar of vinegar may stand next to כמכא.

steps.title: Why is vinegar different from salt?
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי challenges the two answers: why should vinegar be treated differently from salt?
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is the difference?
steps.whatsHappening: רב דימי points out that the two answers seem inconsistent and asks what makes vinegar different from salt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In both cases dairy might fall into a meat seasoning. If the risk is the same, why is one forbidden and the other permitted?

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference? (a challenge that two similar cases were treated differently)

phrases.english: And what is the difference?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַאי שְׁנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the contrast between steps 3 and 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's different rulings for salt and vinegar.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The risk of dairy falling in seems the same, so the rulings should match.

steps.title: רב נחמן: think about it for a long time
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן does not explain directly. He tells רב דימי that after thinking it over at length he will understand.
steps.simpleTranslation: When you eat a כור of salt over it, you will know.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן brushes off the question with a saying, telling רב דימי to think it through for a long time. This sets up the real explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Eating a whole כור of salt takes a very long time, so the saying means 'think about it deeply.' רב נחמן does not give the reason himself; the גמרא supplies it in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: A כור, a very large measure

phrases.english: When you eat over it
a kor of salt?
phrases.notes: A saying meaning 'once you've thought about this for a long time, you'll understand.'

steps.triggerLanguage: לְכִי תֵּיכוּל עֲלַהּ כּוֹרָא דְמִלְחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by putting it off rather than explaining.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No direct reason. The asker is told to think about it at length.

steps.title: In salt the dairy stays visible, in vinegar it dissolves
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains: dairy that falls into salt stays there and can be seen, but dairy that falls into vinegar dissolves away.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? In this case (salt), the forbidden thing stays in its form. In that case (vinegar), the forbidden thing does not stay in its form.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the actual reason for the difference between salt and vinegar.
steps.deeperAnalysis: כמכא that falls into dry salt stays in the salt as real pieces of dairy that can later reach meat. In vinegar the כמכא melts and disappears, so nothing real is left to cause a problem.

keyTerms.meaning: It stays in its form, still really there
It does not stay in its form, it is gone

steps.whatToRemember: Salt next to dairy is forbidden because dairy that falls into salt stays there. Vinegar is allowed because dairy that falls into vinegar dissolves away.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
this one – the forbidden thing remains in its form,
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the salt. Some versions have the words in round brackets, and the square brackets show the corrected wording. Both mean the same.

phrases.english: and that one – the forbidden thing does not remain in its form.
phrases.notes: 'That one' is the vinegar, where the dairy dissolves.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי טַעְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the real answer to the challenge of step 5.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Salt and vinegar carry the same risk, so they should be ruled the same way.
steps.terutzMaskana: In salt the dairy stays in its form, and in vinegar it dissolves, so only salt is forbidden.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Dairy that stays in its form in a meat seasoning is a real concern. Dairy that dissolves away is not.

steps.title: A young bird falls into a jug of dairy dip and is permitted
steps.stepSummary: A young bird fell into a jug of כמכא, and רב חיננא בריה דרבא מפשרוניא permitted it.
steps.simpleTranslation: A young bird fell into a jug of כמכא (a salty dairy dip). רב חיננא, the son of רבא from פשרוניא, permitted it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a real case: meat (a bird) fell into a salty dairy dip, and a rabbi permitted it. This sets up the next steps, which explain why.
steps.deeperAnalysis: כמכא is salty, and שמואל rules that salted food is treated like boiling food, which passes taste. So a bird falling into this salty dairy dip sounds like a clear בשר בחלב problem. The surprise is that it was permitted, and the גמרא will now explain why.

keyTerms.meaning: A salty dairy dip, the same as כּוּתָּחָא

phrases.english: There was a certain young bird
that fell into a jug of kamka,
phrases.notes: כמכא is a salty dip made with milk. A few lines later the גמרא calls the same food כותחא.

phrases.english: Rav Chinnana permitted it,
the son of Rava of Pashronya.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא בַּר גּוֹזָלָא דִּנְפַל לְכַדָּא דְּכַמְכָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from salt-and-כמכא jars to a case where meat actually fell into כמכא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A young bird that fell into כמכא was permitted by רב חיננא בריה דרבא מפשרוניא.

steps.title: רבא praises the ruling
steps.stepSummary: רבא says only someone as wise as רב חיננא could find a way to permit such a case.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Who is wise enough to permit a case like this, if not רב חיננא, the son of רבא from פשרוניא?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא praises the ruling. This tells us the case looked forbidden and it took real wisdom to permit it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's praise shows the leniency was not obvious. It also prepares us for the next step, which spells out the clever reasoning behind the ruling.

phrases.english: Rava said:

phrases.aramaic: מַאן חַכִּים לְמִישְׁרֵי כִּי הַאי גַוְונָא,
phrases.english: Who is wise enough to permit in a case like this,
if not Rav Chinnana,
the son of Rava of Pashronya?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: מַאן חַכִּים לְמִישְׁרֵי כִּי הַאי גַוְונָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Endorses the ruling of step 8.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבא approves of the leniency and praises its author.

steps.title: Why the bird is permitted: the dip is salty but still edible
steps.stepSummary: שמואל's rule 'salted is like boiling' only applies to food too salty to eat. כותחא is still eaten despite its salt, so it does not count as 'boiling'.
steps.simpleTranslation: He holds: when שמואל said 'salted food is like boiling food,' he meant only food so salty it cannot be eaten. But this כותחא is eaten even with its salt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the reasoning behind רב חיננא's ruling and answers the hidden question: doesn't שמואל say salted food is like hot food?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally cold foods touching each other don't pass taste, but שמואל treats salted food like boiling food, which does pass taste. רב חיננא narrows that rule: only food salty enough to be inedible counts as 'boiling'. כותחא is a normal eating food, so here it acts like a plain cold food, and the bird stays permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: Salted food is treated like boiling food (it passes taste)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רב חיננא disagrees with שמואל. He accepts that salted is like boiling. He only explains which level of saltiness the rule covers.

phrases.english: He holds:
when Shmuel said
"a salted food is like a boiling food,"
that applies only where
it cannot be eaten because of its salt,
but this kutach
is eaten despite its salt.

steps.triggerLanguage: קָסָבַר: כִּי אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל מָלִיחַ הֲרֵי הוּא כְּרוֹתֵחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the reasoning that רבא praised.
steps.kashyaTarget: The implied question of how a bird in salty dairy can be permitted given שמואל's rule.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of a rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any salted food counts as 'boiling', so the bird would absorb the dairy.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only food too salty to eat counts as 'boiling'; edible כותחא does not, so the bird is permitted.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical limit of the well-known rule מליח הרי הוא כרותח.

steps.title: The leniency is only for a raw bird
steps.stepSummary: The leniency applies only to a raw bird. A roasted bird needs its outer layer peeled. If it has cracks or was seasoned with spices, all of it is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies only to a raw bird. A roasted one needs peeling. If it has cracks, all of it is forbidden. If it was seasoned with spices, all of it is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא limits the leniency of the bird case. It lists situations where the bird absorbs more of the dairy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The leniency fully covers only a raw, whole, unseasoned bird. Roasting makes the outside absorb, so the outer layer must be peeled off. Cracks or spices let the dairy reach the whole bird, so all of it becomes forbidden.
steps.whatToRemember: The bird in כמכא is fully permitted only if it is raw. A roasted bird needs peeling. A cracked or spiced bird is entirely forbidden.

phrases.english: And this applies only to a raw one,
but a roasted one requires peeling,

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי אִית בֵּיהּ פִּילֵי – כּוּלֵּיהּ אָסוּר,
phrases.english: and if it has cracks, all of it is forbidden,
and if it is seasoned with spices, all of it is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָנֵי מִילֵּי חַי, אֲבָל צָלִי – בָּעֵי קְלִיפָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the leniency explained in step 10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Raw: permitted; roasted: needs peeling; cracked or spiced: entirely forbidden.

steps.title: Bread that meat was cut on is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן quotes שמואל: a loaf of bread that meat was cut on is forbidden to eat.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said in the name of שמואל: a loaf of bread that someone cut meat on is forbidden to eat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new case about one food soaking into another: meat cut on top of bread.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the concern is the meat's blood, not milk. Juice dripping from the meat soaks into the bread, so the bread becomes forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: That one cut meat on top of it
It is forbidden to eat it

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said that Shmuel said:
A loaf on which one cut meat
phrases.notes: He means roasted meat that hasn't been salted, so its blood drips into the bread.

phrases.english: is forbidden to eat,

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן, אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: כִּכָּר שֶׁחָתַךְ עָלֶיהָ בָּשָׂר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: New case on a related theme of foods soaking into one another.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Bread that meat was cut on is forbidden.

steps.title: Three conditions for the bread to be forbidden
steps.stepSummary: The bread is forbidden only if the meat is red, the juice soaked all the way through, and the juice is thick. Thin juice is no problem.
steps.simpleTranslation: This applies only if it is red, and only if it soaked all the way through, and only if it is thick. But if it is thin, we have no problem with it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows שמואל's rule with three conditions. If any condition is missing, the bread is permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each condition makes the rule narrower. The meat must still be red with blood. The juice must have soaked through to the other side of the loaf. The juice must be thick. Thin, runny juice does not make the bread forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: That it passed through to the other side
We have no problem with it

steps.whatToRemember: Bread that meat was cut on is forbidden only if the meat is red, the juice soaked through, and the juice is thick.

phrases.english: and this applies only if it is red,
and this applies only if it passed through,
phrases.notes: The juice soaked so deep that you can see it from both sides of the loaf.

phrases.english: and this applies only if it is thick,
but if it is thin, we have no problem with it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָנֵי מִילֵּי דְּאַסְמֵיק, וְהָנֵי מִילֵּי דְּאַבְרְיֵהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits שמואל's ruling from step 12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Forbidden only if red, soaked through, and thick; thin juice is permitted.

steps.title: What שמואל and רב הונא did with such bread
steps.stepSummary: שמואל would throw such bread to his dog. רב הונא would give it to his attendant.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל would throw it to his dog. רב הונא would give it to his attendant.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports how two sages handled bread that meat was cut on. This sets up the challenge in the next step against רב הונא's practice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל did not eat the bread himself, in line with his ruling. רב הונא also did not eat it, yet he let someone else eat it. That looks inconsistent, and the גמרא will now ask about it.

phrases.english: Shmuel would throw it to his dog,
Rav Huna would give it to his attendant.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁמוּאֵל שָׁדֵי לֵיהּ לְכַלְבֵּיהּ, רַב הוּנָא יָהֵיב לֵיהּ לְשַׁמָּעֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows how sages acted on the bread ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שמואל gave the bread to his dog; רב הונא gave it to his attendant.

steps.title: Either way, רב הונא's practice makes no sense
steps.stepSummary: If the bread is permitted, it is permitted for everyone. If it is forbidden, it is forbidden for everyone. So why did רב הונא give it to his attendant?
steps.simpleTranslation: Whichever way you look at it: if it is permitted, it is permitted for everyone; if it is forbidden, it is forbidden for everyone!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב הונא. A food cannot be forbidden for him and permitted for his attendant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: הלכה is the same for every Jew. If the bread is permitted, רב הונא should eat it himself. If it is forbidden, he may not feed it to his attendant. Either way, his behavior seems wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: Whichever way you look at it

phrases.english: Whichever way you look at it:
if it is permitted, it is permitted for everyone,
if it is forbidden, it is forbidden for everyone!

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה נַפְשָׁךְ? אִי שְׁרֵי – לְכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא שְׁרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב הונא's practice reported in step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא giving the bread to his attendant but not eating it himself.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A dilemma: the same food cannot be permitted for one person and forbidden for another.

steps.title: רב הונא was just squeamish
steps.stepSummary: The bread really was permitted. רב הונא simply had a delicate nature and did not want to eat it himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא is different, because he was squeamish.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. רב הונא avoided the bread out of personal disgust, not because of הלכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer picks the 'permitted' side of the dilemma. The bread was fine for everyone, including רב הונא. He passed it on only because it did not appeal to him.

phrases.english: Rav Huna is different,
because he was squeamish.

steps.triggerLanguage: שָׁאנֵי רַב הוּנָא דַּאֲנִינָא דַּעְתֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the dilemma of step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Personal circumstance, not a difference in הלכה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב הונא avoided the bread because it was forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: The bread was permitted; רב הונא just found it unappetizing.

steps.title: רבא ate the bread and called it 'meat wine'
steps.stepSummary: רבא would eat such bread and call the red juice 'meat wine'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא would eat it, and he called it 'meat wine.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends the topic with רבא's practice: he ate the bread with no hesitation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's practice confirms that the bread, in the permitted cases, was fully allowed. He even treated the juice as a tasty addition, calling it 'meat wine'.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Meat wine', a name for the red meat juice

steps.whatToRemember: In the permitted cases, the bread is fully allowed. רב הונא avoided it only out of squeamishness, and רבא happily ate it.

phrases.english: Rava would eat it,
and he called it "meat wine."
phrases.notes: He means the red juice soaked into the bread. He enjoyed it like wine.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָכֵיל לֵיהּ, וְקָרֵי לֵיהּ חֲמַר בָּשָׂר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of step 16 that the bread is permitted.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: In the permitted cases, bread that meat was cut on may be eaten; רבא ate it gladly.

steps.title: No vessel under roasting meat until the redness is gone
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן quotes שמואל: you may not place a vessel under roasting meat until all of its red appearance is gone.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said in the name of שמואל: You may not put a vessel under meat until all the redness in the meat has disappeared.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new rule from שמואל about putting a dish under meat while it roasts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: As long as the meat is still red, blood may still be dripping out of it. If you catch those drippings in a vessel, blood may fall in with the fat. So you must wait until the redness is completely gone.

keyTerms.meaning: until it is finished, until it is gone

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said that Shmuel said:
One may not place a vessel under meat

phrases.aramaic: עַד שֶׁיִּכְלֶה כׇּל מַרְאֵה אַדְמוּמִית שֶׁבּוֹ.
phrases.english: until all the red appearance in it is gone.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן, אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from bread soaked in meat juice (steps 13-17) to a related case: catching the drippings of roasting meat.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vessel may not be placed under roasting meat until all of the meat's redness is gone.

steps.title: How can we tell when the redness is gone?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how we know when the meat's redness has fully disappeared.
steps.simpleTranslation: How do we know when that has happened?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a practical question about שמואל's rule and sets up the next step, which gives an answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל's rule depends on knowing when the redness is gone. But you cannot easily see inside roasting meat. So the גמרא wants a clear sign.

keyTerms.meaning: from where do we know? how can we tell?

phrases.english: How do we know?

steps.triggerLanguage: מְנָא יָדְעִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how to apply the rule of step 18 in practice.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A practical sign that the meat's redness, meaning its blood, is completely gone.

steps.title: The sign is when smoke rises
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא, quoting רב פפא, says the redness is gone once the meat's smoke rises.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא said in the name of רב פפא: Once its smoke rises.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with a visible sign: when smoke goes up from the meat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Smoke rising shows that the meat has roasted enough. By then, the blood should already be out. So from that point you may put the vessel underneath.

phrases.aramaic: מָר זוּטְרָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב פָּפָּא אָמַר:
phrases.english: Mar Zutra said in the name of Rav Pappa:
Once its smoke rises.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָר זוּטְרָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַב פָּפָּא אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The redness is gone once smoke rises from the meat.

steps.title: Maybe only the bottom is done
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי objects: maybe the bottom of the meat is roasted but the top is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי challenged this: But maybe the lower part of the meat is roasted and the upper part is not?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי attacks רב פפא's smoke sign, saying it does not prove the whole piece of meat is done.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The bottom of the meat is close to the fire, so it roasts first and may start smoking. The top may still be raw and still giving off blood. So smoke rising does not prove that all the blood is out.

keyTerms.meaning: he challenged it, he attacked it

phrases.english: Rav Ashi challenged this:
But perhaps the lower part is done,
and the upper part is not done?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַב אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the sign given in step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב פפא's sign that rising smoke shows all the redness is gone.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The smoke may come from the lower part near the fire, while the upper part is still raw and dripping blood. So the sign is not reliable for the whole piece.

steps.title: There is no sign, so use two lumps of salt
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי concludes there is no reliable sign. The only fix is to throw two lumps of salt into it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב אשי said: There is no fix for it, except to throw two lumps of salt into it.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the smoke sign failed, רב אשי gives a new answer: there is no way to know, but salt can solve the problem. His sentence continues past this section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אשי does not offer a better sign. He says waiting for a sign will never work. Instead, he gives a practical solution using two lumps of salt.

keyTerms.meaning: there is no remedy for it

steps.confusionAlert: רב אשי is not saying the drippings are forbidden no matter what. He is saying there is no sign to rely on, so the solution must come from the salt.

phrases.english: Rather, Rav Ashi said:
There is no remedy for it,

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא מִשְׁדֵּא בֵּיהּ תַּרְתֵּי גַּלְלֵי מִלְחָא,
phrases.english: except to throw two lumps of salt into it,

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After rejecting the smoke sign in step 21, רב אשי replaces רב פפא's answer to the question of step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: There is no reliable sign. The only remedy is to throw two lumps of salt into it.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replaces the rejected answer with a practical fix instead of a sign.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might have thought rising smoke shows that all the blood is gone.
steps.terutzMaskana: No sign is reliable. Salt must be used to fix the problem.
